# Does Google Penalise AI-Assisted Content for Thin Content?

Recently, one of the biggest questions surrounding publishing AI-assisted content has been whether Google penalises it. Google has stated that it doesn’t reward or punish content created by AI, [provided it adds value](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content) and meets Google’s [Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) standards. However, **Google does evaluate the quality and usefulness of AI-assisted content against some strict guidelines**.

This subject was recently spotlighted [by Search Engine Journal](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-may-be-penalizing-ai-generated-content-as-thin-content/583773/). A website owner reported receiving a partial manual action from Google for thin content on a forum section of a website that’s existed for almost 20 years. The forum contains more than half a million posts, with an AI chatbot labelled as a staff member generating over 100,000 replies. While Google hasn’t confirmed that the AI-generated responses caused the penalty specifically, some experts are speculating that the automated AI chatbot replies may have impacted the value of the forum, as one of the main reasons why users visit forums is to read answers based on genuine human experience.

## Understanding Thin Content and Manual Actions

Google has often described thin content as pages that provide little or no value to users, that don’t help answer questions or solve a problem. These pages tend to be shallow or created primarily to rank in search results instead of serving a genuine purpose. Other common examples of thin content that Google looks for include:

*   **Duplicate content** – Content copied or scraped from other websites without adding any original insight or value
*   **Low-quality affiliate pages** – Basic product pages that rely on manufacturer descriptions or affiliate links without providing genuine reviews or comparisons
*   **Doorway pages** – Pages created purely to target specific keywords before directing users elsewhere
*   **Superficial pages** – Surface-level content that doesn’t answer the user’s question.

**Google’s aim is to surface content to users that is genuinely useful and accurate**, so pages that fail to meet these standards may not rank or, in more serious cases, receive a manual action where they’re removed from search results altogether. A manual action means a member of Google’s search team has reviewed a website and determined that it violates Google’s spam policies. Depending on the issue, the action can affect individual pages, a section of a website, or the entire site.

The important thing to note here is that AI doesn’t automatically create thin content. However, **if AI-assisted content is published without editing, fact-checking, adding value, or injecting expertise, it may be flagged as thin content**.

## E-E-A-T Explained

**One reason why thin content performs so poorly and gets penalised is that it often lacks [Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T)](https://herdl.com/understanding-googles-latest-e-e-a-t-and-algorithm-updates/)**. These are signals that Google looks for when assessing whether content is likely to help users. This means the strongest content should demonstrate knowledge of the subject and give readers a tangible reason to choose it over another result.

For experience, content should demonstrate first-hand knowledge. This could include personal experience, original research, unique data, testimonials, or examples from real-world situations. For example, an [SEO agency](https://herdl.com/seo/) writing about a technical SEO migration could explain what happened during a real migration, including the problems they encountered and how they were resolved.

To cover expertise, content should show the information presented is written by someone who understands the subject in-depth. This could mean an author with relevant professional experience, references to credible research, case studies, or displaying or mentioning relevant certifications. For example, an accountant writing about changes to tax regulations could explain how the rules apply to businesses and cite the relevant legislation or official guidance.

The authority pillar of E-E-A-T is based on how others view your expertise. High-quality, relevant websites linking to your content (also known as backlinks), industry peers referencing your work, and users recognising your brand as a reliable source all contribute to your authority. For example, if an ecommerce brand publishes research related to its products and this information is cited in authoritative blogs, the brand has stronger evidence of authority than an ecommerce website publishing generic articles without external recognition.

For trustworthiness, your content and website should be accurate and transparent. Check claims, statistics, and factual information against credible sources. Clear author information, genuine customer reviews, and an honest explanation of who is responsible for your website can also help establish trust. An example you may have seen before is how healthcare websites clearly show their authors and reviewers and provide sources for medical claims to make it easy for readers to understand when the information was last reviewed.

## Best Practices for AI-Assisted Content Generation

AI can be a great accelerator for content creation. However, to produce high-quality content, AI output should serve as the foundation rather than the final product. By incorporating genuine human expertise, unique professional insights and real-world anecdotes, you can upgrade the piece from generic to authoritative. This layer of human oversight – ensuring accuracy, demonstrating E-E-A-T and tailoring the voice to your audience – is essential for creating content that readers find valuable and that meets Google’s quality standards.

If you’re using AI to support your content creation process, here are some best practices to ensure the final result is aligned with Google’s quality expectations:

*   **Focus on user intent** – Answer the primary question thoroughly while also covering related topics readers are likely to search for next
*   **Add original expertise** – Include personal experience, industry-specific knowledge, unique data, or observations that AI doesn’t always provide on its own
*   **Use relatable examples** – Real-world scenarios and analogies can make complex topics easier to understand and add value
*   **Personalise the voice** – Rewrite generic introductions to reflect your unique brand voice and perspective
*   **Cover topics in depth** – Avoid skimming the surface of a topic and leaving knowledge gaps. Search engines look for topic completeness when evaluating content, determining rankings, and citing pages in AI experiences
*   **Provide practical value** – Include step-by-step guides, recommendations, comparison tables, or actionable advice readers can use to make decisions
*   **Fact-check the AI output** – Ensure every AI-generated statistic and claim is accurate before you publish
*   **Remove repetition** – Tighten the AI output by cutting unnecessary filler words and sentences, as well as repeated ideas
*   **Improve readability** – Replace any generic AI-generated headings with descriptive language. Include bullet points and clear formatting so readers can find information and scan your content quickly.

## A Few Ways to Fix Thin Content

Recovering from a manual action for thin content can be difficult, so prevention is always the best option. If parts of your website aren’t providing enough value, there are several practical improvements you can make. However, we recommend getting professional input before making any radical changes to your site or giving all your content a complete overhaul.

### Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Audit

At [Herdl](https://herdl.com/), we conduct [CRO audits](https://herdl.com/cro-fundamentals-that-build-trust-with-website-visitors/) to find actionable opportunities to improve your website. This audit combines insights from analytics, heatmaps, scroll behaviour, and competitor analysis, focusing on the key performance indicators (KPIs) that matter to your business. Whether it’s reducing friction in the conversion funnel or restructuring pages to optimise the user journey, the ultimate goal is to boost the percentage of visitors from passive browsers to active conversions.

### E-E-A-T Audit

Our E-E-A-T audit identifies if your website clearly demonstrates the principles of Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. We evaluate how well your site aligns with the current search landscape and provide a clear action plan for improvement to strengthen your overall visibility against your target audience’s search intents.

## The Final Word

The recent forum case mentioned on Reddit reinforces what Google has been saying for a long time about how quality matters more than how content is created. AI can play a role in content production, but it shouldn’t replace human expertise or oversight. If you’re using AI-assisted content to support your digital marketing and want to check if your pages meet Google’s quality expectations, feel free to [contact us](https://herdl.com/contact/) and let’s chat about it.

items.metadata.title: Patient Acquisition Strategy: 5 Ways To Improve It
items.markdown:
# 5 Ways To Improve It

A strong patient acquisition strategy does more than bring people to your website. It helps them take the next step—booking care—without confusion, delays or extra effort.

At its core, [patient acquisition(this link opens in new window)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31413443/) is the process of attracting new patients and guiding them from initial interest to a completed visit. That includes how easily patients can find you online, how simple it is to access care and how smoothly they move through scheduling, [intake](https://www.phreesia.com/products/registration/) and follow-up.

It’s also closely tied to [retention](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-4-ways-to-boost-patient-loyalty-and-retention/). The same factors that help someone book their first appointment—clear information, easy access and timely communication—are often what bring them back.

That’s why patient acquisition marketing can’t sit in a silo. It has to connect with the operational workflows that shape the patient experience day-to-day.

In this article, we’ll break down five practical ways to improve your patient acquisition strategy, including:

*   Better online visibility
*   Easier scheduling
*   Stronger [referral conversion](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-3-patient-referrals-process-pain-points-and-how-to-solve-them/)
*   Clear and timely communication
*   Measurement and follow-through

Together, these levers reflect how acquisition actually happens across the patient journey, plus where small improvements can lead to more booked appointments without adding more work for your team.

![5 ways to improve your patient acquisition strategy infographic](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/PatientAcquisition-Recap.png "PatientAcquisition - Recap")

## Patient acquisition strategy starts with the right foundation

A patient acquisition strategy works best when it’s built around how patients actually move through the healthcare experience. At a practical level, that strategy includes a few [connected pieces(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8913063/):

*   **Visibility:** Can patients find you when they’re searching for care?
*   **Access:** Can they quickly see availability and understand how to book?
*   **Conversion:** Can they move from interest to a scheduled appointment without friction?
*   **Retention:** Do they have a positive experience that brings them back?
*   **Follow-through:** Are there systems in place to keep [patients engaged](https://www.phreesia.com/products/patient-engagement/) after that first visit?

When any one of these steps breaks down, new patient acquisition [becomes harder(this link opens in new window)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1057/s41271-025-00612-7). For example, a patient might find your organization online, but hit a dead end trying to schedule. Or they might get referred, but never hear back in time to book. All that to say: The demand is often there, but the experience creates friction that slows everything down—or shuts it down entirely.

That’s why patient acquisition strategies need to go beyond marketing campaigns. They should connect directly to the workflows that shape access, scheduling and communication behind the scenes.

And the most effective patient marketing strategy is one that reduces effort on both sides. Patients can quickly find what they need and take action, while staff spend less time chasing paperwork, managing manual follow-ups or filling gaps in the process.

![The foundation for patient acquisition infographic](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/PatientAcquisition-Foundation.png "PatientAcquisition - Foundation")

## 1\. Improve online visibility and reputation to support patient acquisition marketing

For many patients, the search for care starts online. And it’s often quick: just a few searches, a handful of tabs and a decision. What they find in those first moments can determine whether they move forward or move on.

That first impression is built on a few key elements, including:

*   **Online reviews:** This is key—[up to 60% of people(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6526774/) rely on reviews when choosing a provider. In addition to star ratings, patients are looking for signals that others felt heard, respected and cared for. A steady stream of recent, authentic feedback can quietly tip the scale in your favor.
*   **Provider profiles:** Patients want to quickly understand who they’ll be seeing, what conditions are treated and whether the provider takes their insurance. When that information is incomplete, outdated or buried, it creates friction at the moment patients are trying to make a decision.
*   **Your website:** This is your [digital front door](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-the-digital-front-door-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters/). Your site should clearly explain services, locations and insurance coverage, and make next steps obvious. If patients have to hunt for basic details or figure out on their own how to book, many won’t stick around.

Across all of these touchpoints, accuracy and consistency matter more than most teams realize. When provider details, availability and insurance information line up across your website, search listings and third-party platforms, it makes things feel clear and dependable from the start. That goes a long way in building trust.

[Patient satisfaction surveys](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-patient-satisfaction-surveys-how-and-why-to-use-them/) and review generation can build on that over time. When you’re regularly [collecting feedback(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10048416/) and making it easy for satisfied patients to share their experiences, it adds a layer of credibility that feels genuine.

## 2\. Make new patient acquisition easier with online scheduling

[Online scheduling(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12081397/) often makes the difference between a patient booking or not booking at all.

Put yourself in the patients’ shoes: They’ve just decided they want care. Maybe they’re on your website or they found you through search. They’re ready to act. But if the only option is to call during business hours, wait on hold or remember to follow up later, that momentum can disappear quickly.

In fact, most patients [don’t want to call(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11489984/). They want to book right then and move on with their day. And if they can’t, many won’t come back.

That’s why [online scheduling](https://www.phreesia.com/products/appointments/) is such a powerful driver of new patient acquisition. It meets patients in the moment they’re ready and gives them a clear next step.

“Don’t overcomplicate the questions that you ask through online self-scheduling,” advises Amy Williamson, director of clinical operations at [Bluegrass Orthopaedics(this link opens in new window)](https://www.bluegrassortho.com/). “Think about it from a patient perspective, not the provider’s perspective.”

Where you place scheduling matters just as much as offering it in the first place. It should be easy to find anywhere a patient might decide to book, including:

*   Your website
*   Provider profiles
*   Search listings
*   Social channels

The experience itself also needs to feel connected and easy. When scheduling interfaces directly with your EHR and shows [real-time availability(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8796867/), patients can book with confidence and staff don’t have to spend time cleaning up mismatched appointments or playing phone tag.

“Make it clear and easy for patients,” says Williamson. “Have a platform that makes it simple to schedule online and doesn’t require them to call your office with follow-up questions.”

## 3\. Turn referrals into booked appointments faster

[Patient referrals](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-patient-referrals/) are one of the strongest signals of intent you can get. By the time a patient is referred, they already know they need care and are ready to take the next step.

But ironically, that’s often where things slow down.

In many organizations, [referral workflows(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10863292/) are still pretty manual. Paper forms, e-faxes, disconnected systems and delayed follow-up can create friction at exactly the wrong moment. Referrals sit in queues, staff have to track down missing details and patients are left waiting or wondering what they’re supposed to do next.

From the patient’s perspective, [that’s confusing(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12096378/). They’ve been told to schedule, but don’t always know how, when or with whom. Some will follow up. But others get busy, lose track or start looking elsewhere. And those missed connections can quickly turn into lost visits—and revenue.

The good news is, small changes can make a big difference. When [referral workflows are centralized(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12869834/) and easier to track, teams can quickly see what’s moving and what’s stuck. That makes follow-up more timely and a lot less manual.

It also helps to give patients a clearer path forward. Instead of waiting for a call, they can be guided to schedule sooner, with fewer steps and less uncertainty.

And when referrals move smoothly, it shows. Patients get into care faster, staff spend less time chasing information and more of those high-intent referrals turn into actual visits.

## 4\. Match the patient experience to your patient marketing strategy

A strong patient marketing strategy [sets expectations(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11040877/). So the experience that follows should live up to them.

“\[This\] establishes trust early on in the experience, which translates to trust in the practitioners and staff,” explains Williamson.

For instance, if a patient finds you through a polished website or a clear message about easy access, they expect that same level of clarity when they try to book, complete forms or follow up. When those pieces don’t match, it creates friction and distrust—and that can determine whether they move forward or come back.

This is where acquisition and retention start to overlap. Yes, the first visit is about getting someone in the door. But it’s also about making the experience smooth enough that they want to come back.

A few elements make a big difference here:

*   **Timely communication:** This helps patients understand what to expect and what to do next, reducing uncertainty.
*   **Clear next steps:** Clarity makes scheduling, intake and follow-up easier to navigate without confusion.
*   **Easy intake:** When pre-visit tasks can be done quickly online or on a mobile device, patients are more likely to follow through.
*   **Thoughtful touchpoints:** Things like [well-timed reminders](https://www.phreesia.com/patient-appointment-reminders), simple pre-visit forms and clear follow-up messages help the experience feel smooth and connected.

## 5\. Measure what your patient acquisition strategies are actually driving

It’s easy to focus on activity: more campaigns, more traffic, more referrals. But if you’re not tying that back to booked appointments, it’s hard to know what’s actually working.

According to Williamson, a strong patient-centric acquisition and [appointment strategy](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-how-to-create-a-patient-centric-appointment-strategy/) comes down to a few key metrics that connect effort to outcomes:

*   **New patient appointments:** How many first-time visits are being scheduled
*   **Scheduling conversion rate:** How often patients who start booking actually finish
*   **Referral conversion rate:** How many referred patients turn into scheduled visits
*   **Review volume:** Whether you’re consistently building feedback and visibility
*   **Patient satisfaction signals:** What patients are saying about their experience

Looking at these together helps you quickly spot where things are breaking down. Strong traffic but low scheduling conversion? There may be friction in the booking experience. High referral volume but low conversion? Follow-up may be too slow or inconsistent.

It’s also worth looking beyond volume into what’s actually driving growth. While some channels may bring in more patients overall, others bring in patients who are more likely to follow through and [stay engaged(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483965/).

When you measure across the full journey, it becomes much easier to adjust what’s not working. Often, small changes—like making scheduling easier or tightening referral follow-up—can lead to more booked visits.

![How to measure patient acquisition: the KPIs that matter infographic](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/PatientAcquisition-KPIs.png "PatientAcquisition - KPIs")

## How AI is changing patient acquisition

[Automation](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-15-benefits-of-automation-in-healthcare/) has helped healthcare organizations streamline scheduling and outreach for years. Now, [AI is taking that a step further(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11047988/) by helping teams make smarter decisions across the entire patient journey.

Here’s how:

*   **Converting interest, not just capturing it:** Traditional digital tools helped organizations generate leads and appointment requests. AI can now help identify which patients are most likely to schedule, personalize follow-up and reduce the drop-off that happens between interest and action.
*   **Smarter scheduling and access:** [AI-powered scheduling tools](https://www.phreesia.com/appointmentaccelerator/) can help match patients with the right provider, location or appointment type faster, while also helping organizations optimize availability and reduce gaps in the schedule.
*   **More proactive referral management:** AI can help prioritize referrals, identify delays and surface patients who may be at risk of falling through the cracks, helping teams follow up sooner and move patients into care faster.
*   **More personalized outreach and engagement:** AI can support more targeted communication based on patient preferences and behavior, so outreach feels more relevant and timely.
*   **Conversational AI for scheduling and patient access:** [AI voice](https://www.phreesia.com/products/phreesia-voiceai/) and chat tools are increasingly helping patients schedule appointments, ask questions and navigate next steps without waiting on hold or relying entirely on staff availability.
*   **Connected intelligence across the patient journey:** The biggest gains come from connected systems that understand what’s happening across scheduling, referrals, communication and follow-up. When those pieces work together, organizations get a clearer view of where patients are getting stuck and how to keep them moving forward.

## The bottom line

A strong patient acquisition strategy makes it easier for patients to move forward. When patients can find you, understand their options and book without jumping through hoops, more of that initial interest turns into real appointments. And when the experience feels smooth from the start, they’re much more likely to come back.

The organizations seeing the most consistent growth are simply connecting the dots—making sure visibility, scheduling, referrals and follow-up all work together. In most cases, the demand is already there. When the path to booking is clear, everything else starts to fall into place.

## Frequently asked questions

Online scheduling gives patients a simple, immediate way to book care when they’re ready. By removing the need to call or wait for office hours, it reduces drop-off and helps more patients follow through with scheduling.

Referrals are one of the clearest signals that a patient is ready for care. But if the process feels slow or unclear, it’s easy for that momentum to stall. When referral workflows are more streamlined, it’s much easier for patients to follow through and get scheduled.

Patient acquisition focuses on attracting new patients and getting them to book their first visit. Patient retention focuses on keeping patients engaged over time. In practice, the two are closely connected, since a smooth first experience often leads to ongoing care.

# AI assessment platforms vs. traditional testing

Something quietly broke in traditional hiring, and most companies felt it before they could name it. Resumes filtered for pedigree, not performance. Standardized tests measured test-taking, not capability. 

AI assessment platforms emerged to close that gap—bringing measurable, simulation-based evaluation into a process long overdue for an upgrade.

This guide breaks down the core differences between AI assessment platforms and traditional testing methods for new roles. By understanding both approaches, you can choose the right strategy to build a stronger, more capable team.

**AI assessment platforms vs. traditional testing snapshot:**

AI assessment platforms evaluate candidates using real-world simulations, structured interviews, and data-driven scoring. Traditional testing relies on static questions, legacy resume screening, and manual evaluation. While AI platforms are designed to measure job-relevant skills and accurately predict future performance, traditional methods often assess theoretical knowledge in isolation.

## **What are AI assessment platforms?**

[AI assessment platforms](https://codesignal.com/technical-assessments/) use artificial intelligence to evaluate candidates through interactive simulations, coding environments, structured interviews, and automated scoring. They heavily focus on skills-based hiring rather than relying on degrees or past job titles.

The key components of these platforms include:

*   **Real-world tasks**, such as live coding, complex problem-solving, and role-specific simulations, role-plays, writing briefs, and analyzing financial data.
*   **AI-assisted or strictly structured interviews** that keep conversations focused on relevant competencies
*   **Automated, standardized scoring** that removes human error from the grading process
*   **Deep performance analytics** and benchmarking to compare candidates objectively

AI testing and assessment platforms use AI to automate test creation, expand coverage for recruiters and hiring teams, and adapt assessments as requirements change. These steps reduce manual effort without sacrificing a thorough (and positive) candidate experience.

**How CodeSignal shines:** CodeSignal takes this a step further. An [AI Interviewer](https://codesignal.com/ai-interviewer/) holds structured conversations, while certified [business](https://codesignal.com/business-assessments/) and [technical assessments](https://codesignal.com/technical-assessments/) tie directly back to real-world skills. Recruiters can then use a standardized skills report to ensure consistent evaluation across the entire talent pool.

## **What is traditional candidate testing?**

Traditional candidate testing refers to the legacy hiring methods historically used to evaluate applicants. These formats were originally built for scale, allowing companies to filter through large volumes of applicants quickly.

**Common formats include**:

*   Multiple-choice tests
*   Manual resume screening
*   Unstructured interviews that vary wildly from candidate to candidate
*   Brain-teaser or puzzle-based coding questions

Traditional testing relies heavily on hands-on assessments, evaluator judgment, and manual review. Depending on the role, this might include coding exercises evaluated through black box testing (assessing outputs and problem-solving results) or white box testing (reviewing code quality, logic, and implementation). 

For business-focused roles, it could involve evaluating sales calls, customer support interactions, case studies, presentations, or role-playing exercises to assess communication, decision-making, and job-specific skills.

The limitations of these methods are significant. Traditional testing primarily measures theoretical knowledge rather than applied skills. Scoring remains highly inconsistent across different interviewers, leading to a high risk of unconscious bias. 

Additionally, these abstract puzzles often result in a frustrating candidate experience. In part, that’s because traditional testing involves many repetitive tasks and redundant test cases, which can be time-consuming and more likely to end in errors.

## **Differences between AI assessment platforms and traditional testing**

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feature** | **AI Assessment Platforms** | **Traditional Testing** |
| **Evaluation method** | Real-world simulations | Static questions |
| **Scoring** | Automated and standardized | Manual and subjective |
| **Skill measurement** | Job-relevant skills | Theoretical knowledge |
| **Candidate experience** | Interactive and realistic | Often repetitive or abstract |
| **Bias control** | Structured and consistent | Varies by interviewer |
| **Predictive power** | High (performance-based) | Limited |

## **Why traditional testing and human judgment fall short in modern hiring**

Legacy hiring has a foundational problem: it measures the wrong things. A brain-teaser score doesn’t predict whether someone will produce quality work, handle ambiguity, or collaborate under pressure. The tools were built for scale and administrative convenience rather than accuracy.

The inconsistency compounds the problem. The same candidate can pass with one manager and fail with another. This isn’t because their skills changed, but because the evaluation did. 

For recruiters and hiring teams, the cost is real: repeated unstructured interviews, high overhead on large test suites, and assessments that falter when tangible job requirements change. All that effort produces a weak signal and might be nearly useless for predicting who will actually succeed in the role.

Traditional testing wasn’t designed to answer the question that matters most: _can this person do the job?_ It was designed to produce a score.

## **How AI assessment platforms improve hiring outcomes**

AI assessment platforms and intelligent test automation help hiring teams evaluate candidates more accurately. This happens by measuring the skills, behaviors, and competencies that predict on-the-job success.

### **Measure real-world performance**

Candidates complete tasks that closely mirror actual daily job work. This provides a significantly better signal of on-the-job success compared to theoretical quizzing.

### **Standardize evaluation across candidates**

Every applicant faces the same questions and the same scoring framework. This consistency drastically reduces interviewer variability and levels the playing field.

### **Increase efficiency without sacrificing quality**

Automated grading and accelerated test execution allow recruiting teams to move faster. AI assessment platforms enable faster and more scalable candidate screening, letting you screen candidates at scale without tying up your hiring team’s valuable time.

### **Improve the candidate experience**

A positive candidate experience is crucial when you want to attract top-tier talent. Job-relevant evaluations often feel more engaging and transparent than traditional screening methods, which allows candidates to showcase their abilities while giving employers more meaningful insights.

### **Support compliance and fairness**

Structured interviews and transparent scoring help organizations align with emerging regulations, like NYC Local Law 144, and evolving AI governance standards.

## **When does traditional testing still make sense?**

There are a few scenarios where traditional testing methods still hold some value. Early-stage companies with very low hiring volumes might not need a comprehensive platform right out of the gate. 

Roles that require only basic knowledge validation, rather than complex problem-solving, can sometimes rely on simple quizzes.

Even in these situations, however, structured and skills-based approaches typically outperform legacy recruiting methods.

## **Common use cases for AI testing tools and assessment platforms**

AI assessment platforms deliver the greatest value in complex, high-volume, and high-stakes hiring scenarios where traditional screening methods struggle to accurately evaluate candidate skills, predict job performance, or scale efficiently. By automating assessments and generating data-driven insights, these platforms help organizations make more informed hiring decisions while reducing time-to-hire and improving candidate quality.

AI assessment platforms are particularly effective in the following use cases:

*   **Technical hiring:** Evaluating engineering, data science, and specialized IT talent
*   **High-volume hiring pipelines:** Managing graduate programs or rapid scaling phases without losing quality
*   **Remote or distributed teams:** Standardizing the hiring process across different time zones and locations
*   **Skills-first hiring initiatives:** Transitioning away from degree-based requirements toward actual capability assessments

AI assessment platforms enable greater test coverage and continuous testing, helping organizations increase test coverage in complex hiring scenarios.

## **What to look for in an AI assessment platform**

Some platforms focus primarily on coding tests, while others provide organization-wide, end-to-end candidate evaluation, structured interviews, skills assessments, and predictive hiring insights. When evaluating software for your recruitment stack, look beyond flashy AI features and focus on tools that help you identify top talent, reduce hiring bias, improve decision-making, and create a positive candidate experience.

Look for these essential features:

*   **Real-world, job-relevant tasks** that mirror the responsibilities candidates will perform on the job, such as coding projects, role plays, data analysis, written exercises, or role-specific assessments.
*   **Robust structured interview capabilities** that help interviewers ask consistent questions, evaluate candidates fairly, and generate more objective hiring feedback.
*   **Transparent, standardized scoring** so hiring teams understand how candidates are evaluated and can make decisions based on clear, defensible criteria.
*   **Benchmarking capabilities across large candidate pools** that allow recruiters and hiring managers to compare candidate performance against peers, previous applicants, or established hiring benchmarks.
*   **Seamless integration with your existing ATS and workflows** to reduce administrative work, centralize hiring data, and streamline collaboration between recruiters and hiring managers.
*   **A demonstrably strong candidate experience** that includes intuitive assessments, mobile-friendly interfaces, clear instructions, accessibility features, and timely communication throughout the hiring process.
*   **Integrated AI assistant capabilities** that help hiring teams generate interview questions, summarize candidate performance, identify skill gaps, surface insights, and reduce manual administrative work throughout the hiring process.
*   **Automated cheating and fraud detection features** that identify suspicious behavior, verify candidate identity, and help maintain assessment integrity without creating unnecessary friction for legitimate candidates.

The best AI assessment platforms combine these capabilities into a single, easy-to-use solution that helps organizations evaluate candidates more effectively, make better hiring decisions, and scale recruitment efforts without sacrificing quality or fairness.

## **Best practices for adopting AI assessment platforms**

Implementing an AI assessment platform is about more than adding new technology to your hiring process. To maximize results, organizations need clear hiring goals, defined success metrics, and the right balance between AI-driven insights and human judgment. 

Following these best practices can help hiring teams make better decisions, improve efficiency, and create a more consistent candidate experience.

### **Identify high-impact use cases first**

Start by identifying where AI-powered testing can have the greatest impact on your organization. Common examples include:

*   Screening high-volume applicant pools
*   Standardizing skills assessments across teams and locations
*   Automating interview scheduling, question generation, or candidate summaries
*   Identifying candidates with the strongest role-specific skills
*   Reducing time-to-hire for hard-to-fill positions

Starting with the highest-impact hiring workflows helps organizations demonstrate value quickly while building confidence in the platform.

### **Establish clear KPIs and success metrics**

Define measurable goals before implementation so you can track progress over time. Common KPIs include:

*   Time-to-hire
*   Assessment completion rates
*   Recruiter time saved
*   Interview-to-offer conversion rates
*   Quality of hire
*   Candidate satisfaction or candidate experience scores

Reviewing these metrics regularly helps teams understand whether the platform is improving hiring outcomes and where additional optimization is needed.

### **Invest in training and adoption**

AI tools are most effective when teams understand how to use them. Provide training that helps QA professionals:

*   Interpret AI-generated candidate insights
*   Validate recommendations before making hiring decisions
*   Recognize potential bias or limitations in AI outputs
*   Incorporate AI into existing recruiting workflows

This ensures teams can make informed decisions rather than relying on automation alone.

### **Use a hybrid approach**

The most successful organizations combine AI-powered testing with traditional testing methods. A hybrid approach allows teams to leverage automation for speed and scale while preserving the strengths of human expertise.

AI can excel at:

*   Screening large applicant pools
*   Summarizing interview feedback
*   Identifying patterns across candidate performance
*   Automating repetitive recruiting tasks
*   Standardizing evaluation criteria

Human recruiters and hiring managers remain essential for:

*   Evaluating communication and interpersonal skills
*   Assessing culture and team fit
*   Investigating unique candidate experiences
*   Making nuanced hiring decisions
*   Building relationships with candidates

The most successful organizations use AI to enhance—not replace—human decision-making. By combining AI-powered assessments with experienced recruiters and hiring managers, companies can make more consistent hiring decisions while improving efficiency and maintaining a positive candidate experience.

## **The future of candidate evaluation is here**

**AI assessment platforms are shifting hiring away from resumes and subjective impressions toward objective, skills-based evaluations that measure real-world performance.**

By combining AI-powered analysis with job-relevant assessments—including non functional testing and stress testing—organizations can make more informed hiring decisions and gain a clearer picture of candidate potential.

If you’re looking to improve hiring accuracy, reduce bias, and identify top talent more efficiently, the right AI assessment platform can provide a significant competitive advantage.

\>> [Chat with a CodeSignal expert today.](https://codesignal.com/demo)

## **Frequently Asked Questions**

### **What is an AI assessment platform?**

An AI assessment platform evaluates candidates using simulations, structured interviews, and automated scoring to measure real-world skills accurately.

### **How is AI hiring better than traditional testing?**

AI hiring provides more accurate, consistent, and job-relevant evaluations. This improves final hiring decisions while delivering a much better candidate experience.

### **Are AI powered testing tools biased?**

Well-designed AI assessments actively reduce bias by standardizing questions and the scoring rubric, though active governance and human oversight remain important.

### **Do AI assessments replace interviews?**

No. They enhance existing interviews by making them more structured, consistent, and data-driven.

### **What industries benefit most from AI assessment platforms?**

Technical roles, high-volume hiring teams, and any organization actively adopting skills-based hiring benefit the most from these platforms.

# 4 Reasons to Implement Contactless Patient Intake

Contactless patient intake has moved well beyond its pandemic-era roots. For many healthcare organizations, it’s now a core part of how they simplify access, reduce front-desk strain and create a smoother start to every visit.

At a basic level, [contactless patient intake(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11440562/) lets patients handle registration, forms and check-in on their own device—often before they walk through the door. Instead of filling out paperwork in the waiting room, they can update insurance, sign consents and review their information from their mobile phone, tablet or computer.

But this isn’t just a digital version of clipboards. It’s more like a [digital front door](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-the-digital-front-door-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters/) that brings together registration, electronic patient intake forms, insurance verification and payments into one connected workflow. That means [less manual work(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8459217/) for staff and fewer gaps or delays to manage. And for patients, it simply feels easier.

Here’s why that shift continues to matter—plus why more organizations are making contactless intake a standard part of how they operate.

## Why contactless patient intake still matters

Contactless patient intake still matters because it addresses the day-to-day challenges that slow practices and frustrate patients.

> “Ultimately, contactless intake enables us to deliver a more efficient, patient-centered experience while strengthening our financial and operational performance across the organization”

Here’s where it makes a real difference:

*   **Patients can complete tasks before they arrive:** Registration, electronic patient intake forms, insurance updates, consents and payments can all happen [ahead of time(this link opens in new window)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/digital-health/articles/10.3389/fdgth.2025.1554762/full). That means fewer delays at check-in and a more predictable start to the visit.
*   **Front-desk workflows become easier to manage:** Instead of juggling paperwork, scanning forms and chasing missing information for every single patient, staff can focus on the exceptions.
*   [**Data is more accurate**(this link opens in new window)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK616906/) **from the start:** When patients enter their own information digitally, it reduces transcription errors and missing fields. Cleaner data upfront helps prevent downstream issues with billing, eligibility and follow-up.
*   **Patients move through check-in faster:** Contactless patient check-in [reduces lines, waiting room congestion(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672792/) and repetitive questions. Patients spend less time filling out forms and more time getting to their appointment.
*   **The intake process feels more like the rest of healthcare:** Patients increasingly expect mobile-first, self-service options. A [digital intake experience(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11440562/) aligns with how they already book appointments, message providers and manage their care.
*   **Teams gain better visibility into intake progress:** With [digital patient check-in systems](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-8-reasons-healthcare-providers-need-digital-patient-check-in/), staff can see who has completed forms, who still needs reminders and where bottlenecks are happening.

## Reason 1: Contactless patient intake reduces friction at registration and check-in

For many practices, the biggest intake challenges still show up at the front desk: long lines, repeated paperwork and last-minute scrambling to collect missing information. Contactless patient intake helps smooth out those pressure points before patients even arrive.

With contactless patient registration, patients can complete their information ahead of time—think reviewing demographics, updating insurance and signing forms on their own device. By the time they get to the office, much of the administrative work is already done.

That shift makes contactless patient check-in [faster and more predictable(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8459217/). Instead of handing out clipboards and re-entering data, staff can focus on confirming details and helping patients who need extra support.

The result: a check-in process that feels more organized and less rushed for both patients and staff.

And those small improvements add up. A smoother start to the visit helps reduce waiting room congestion, keeps schedules on track and creates a better first impression before the clinical encounter even begins.

## Reason 2: Contactless patient intake helps staff work more efficiently

Front-desk and patient access teams are often balancing a [long list of responsibilities(this link opens in new window)](https://diabeticstudies.org/index.php/RDS/article/view/1390/1228)—answering phones, checking patients in, updating records, verifying insurance and handling last-minute issues. With manual intake, those tasks pile up quickly and pull staff in multiple directions at once.

Contactless patient intake helps [streamline that workload(this link opens in new window)](https://www.jmir.org/2021/9/e26189/).

“Utilizing digital intake forms makes data transfer easier to manage for the front-office staff,” says Moore. “By allowing the patients to complete their intake on their own time, they are less rushed with completion and can spend more time verifying and validating what is entered.”

That reduces repetitive data entry and cuts down on back-and-forth with patients to fix missing or incomplete details.

It also reduces the need for follow-up calls and reminders. [Automated outreach(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4831598/)—like appointment reminders, prompts to complete [electronic patient intake forms](https://www.phreesia.com/electronic-intake-forms/) or updates about check-in status—helps keep patients on track without adding more tasks to the front desk’s plate.

Just as important, digital intake makes it easier to manage what’s coming in. Instead of treating every patient the same, staff can quickly see who has completed their forms, who still needs help and where issues might slow things down. That visibility allows teams to prioritize their time more effectively.

The payoff: a more manageable workflow overall. And in a time when staffing constraints are a reality for many organizations, that kind of efficiency can make a meaningful difference.

## Reason 3: Electronic patient intake forms improve data quality and financial readiness

When something goes wrong at intake, it rarely stays contained. Missing or inaccurate information can lead to eligibility issues, billing delays and extra follow-up work after the visit.

[Electronic patient intake forms(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8459217/) help prevent those problems at the source, according to Moore.

Instead of relying on handwritten paperwork or manual entry, patients enter their information directly into digital forms. That [reduces transcription errors(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12574785/) and makes it easier to catch missing details before the visit even starts, he explains. Built-in prompts and required fields also help ensure key information—like demographics, insurance and medical history—is more complete.

[For staff(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9748536/), that means fewer surprises later. With cleaner data upfront, it’s easier to verify coverage, confirm eligibility and prepare for the visit without scrambling to fill in gaps.

There’s a [financial upside(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11219169/), too. When accurate information is captured earlier, teams can estimate patient responsibility more confidently, collect payments sooner and avoid claim denials or delays tied to incorrect or incomplete data.

## Reason 4: Contactless intake supports the patient journey that patients now expect

Patients are used to doing everything from their phone on their own time, without extra steps. Intake is starting to follow that same pattern.

Contactless patient intake [makes it easy(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11440562/) to complete registration, forms and contactless [patient check-in](https://www.phreesia.com/patient-check-in/) in a way that fits into a patient’s day. They can take care of it at home, between meetings or on the go without needing to arrive early or sit in the waiting room filling out paperwork.

That flexibility works across visit types. For in-person care, it means a faster, smoother arrival. For virtual or hybrid visits, it helps ensure patients are ready before the appointment even starts.

Just as important is [how simple the process feels(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9389377/). The best intake experiences don’t require patients to download an app or keep track of another login. Instead, they can open a secure link, complete what’s needed and move on. That lower-friction approach makes it more likely patients actually finish intake and reduces the need for staff to chase down missing information.

![4 reasons to go contactless with patient intake](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ContactlessPatientIntake-4-Reasons-v2.png "ContactlessPatientIntake - 4 Reasons - v2")

## What strong contactless patient intake systems should include

Not all contactless patient intake systems are created equal. Digitizing forms is just one element—the ultimate goal is to create a process that’s easy to complete and easy to manage.

Here are the [capabilities(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9389377/) that matter most:

*   **Mobile-friendly, intuitive design:** Forms should be simple to complete on any device, so patients can finish intake without friction.
*   **Low-friction access:** Patients should be able to open a secure link, complete intake and move on without extra steps that slow them down or lead to drop-off.
*   **Built-in validation and required fields:** [Real-time checks](https://www.phreesia.com/products/eligibility-verification/) help ensure information is complete and usable before the visit.
*   **Secure, reliable data handling:** Patient information should be protected while moving seamlessly into the right systems.
*   [**Integration**](https://www.phreesia.com/products/integrations/) **with existing systems:** Intake data should flow directly into the EHR and related workflows without duplicate entry.
*   **Automated reminders and notifications:** With [automation](https://www.phreesia.com/blog-15-benefits-of-automation-in-healthcare/), patients get prompts to complete intake and stay on track, without adding manual work for staff.
*   **Flexible workflows:** Intake should adapt to different visit types and patient scenarios without creating separate processes.
*   **Clear visibility into intake status:** Staff should be able to quickly see what’s complete, what’s missing and where attention is needed.

![The contactless intake checklist infographic](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ContactlessPatientIntake-Checklist.png "ContactlessPatientIntake - Checklist")

## How AI is changing contactless patient intake

Healthcare organizations have used automation to digitize registration and check-in for years. Now, [AI is helping teams(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11047988/) make intake workflows more responsive, proactive and connected across the entire patient journey with:

*   **Smarter intake completion and follow-up:** Traditional digital intake tools help patients complete forms online. AI can help identify which patients are most likely to leave intake incomplete and trigger [reminders](https://www.phreesia.com/patient-appointment-reminders) or follow-up before missing information becomes a problem at check-in.
*   **More accurate data collection:** AI-assisted workflows can help flag missing, inconsistent or incomplete information in real time, reducing manual review and helping teams catch issues earlier in the process.
*   **More personalized patient communication:** AI can support more targeted outreach based on appointment type, patient behavior or communication preferences, helping reminders and intake prompts feel more timely and relevant.
*   **Better visibility into operational bottlenecks:** AI-powered [analytics](https://www.phreesia.com/products/analytics-and-reports/) can help organizations identify where patients are dropping off during intake, where delays tend to happen and which workflows may need adjustment.
*   [**Conversational AI**](https://www.phreesia.com/products/phreesia-voiceai/) **for patient access:** AI voice and chat tools are increasingly helping patients complete intake tasks, ask questions and navigate next steps without needing to wait on hold or rely entirely on front-desk staff availability.
*   **Connected workflows across the intake journey:** The biggest improvements happen when [scheduling](https://www.phreesia.com/products/appointments/), registration, intake forms, insurance verification, communication and payments work together in one connected system. That gives organizations a clearer view of the entire intake process, and fewer gaps between steps.

## How to implement contactless patient intake successfully

Rolling out contactless patient intake is easier when you treat it like a workflow improvement, not just a technology project.

“Successful implementation starts with communication of the ‘why’ behind making the transition,” says Moore. “Change is hard, so \[it’s\] helpful to explain how the change will impact the organization. Staff workflow positivity is crucial to the implementation.”

After that, a step-by-step approach helps you solve the biggest pain points first and build from there. Here’s how to do it:

*   **Map your current intake process:** Start by looking at the full intake journey. Identify where patients get stuck, where staff spend the most time and where information is often missing or duplicated.
*   **Prioritize the highest-friction steps first:** Focus on the parts of intake most likely to slow things down. These are often the easiest places to create early wins.
*   **Move key tasks upstream:** Give patients the ability to complete forms, update insurance and handle other intake steps before the visit. That helps reduce front-desk bottlenecks and makes arrivals more predictable.
*   **Build workflows for different visit types:** Your intake process should work for more than one scenario. Make sure it can support scheduled visits, higher-volume days and virtual or hybrid care without creating extra manual work.
*   **Keep the experience simple for patients:** [Reduce unnecessary friction(this link opens in new window)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9389377/) wherever you can. A mobile-friendly process with secure link-based access can make it easier for patients to complete intake without downloading an app or managing another login.
*   **Measure what’s working:** After rollout, track practical metrics like intake completion rates, staff follow-up needs and time saved at check-in. Those signals can help you spot gaps, improve adoption and keep refining the process over time.

![Best practices for implementing contactless patient intake infographic](https://www.phreesia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ContactlessPatientIntake-Best-Practices.png "ContactlessPatientIntake - Best Practices")

## Frequently asked questions

Contactless patient intake is a digital process that allows patients to complete registration, forms and check-in on their own device—often before they arrive for their appointment. This can include updating personal details, verifying insurance, signing consents and making payments without relying on in-office paperwork.

A patient intake form is how practices gather the basic information they need before a visit—things like contact details, insurance, medical history and consent forms. When it’s digital, patients can take care of it ahead of time and that information goes straight into the system instead of needing to be re-entered later.

Contactless patient check-in typically starts with a secure link sent by text or email. Patients use that link to confirm their information, complete any remaining forms and check in from their phone. When they arrive, there’s little or nothing left to complete at the front desk.

## Conclusion

Contactless patient intake has evolved into a practical way to simplify how patients register, check-in and prepare for their visits. At the same time, it helps staff manage intake more efficiently. The impact shows up quickly: smoother check-ins, less manual work, more accurate data and an experience that feels easier for patients (and staff) from the start.

For healthcare organizations, the opportunity goes beyond replacing paper forms. It’s about building a connected intake workflow that supports patient access, operational efficiency and financial performance—all without adding complexity.
